units.sourceHTML: 2 Introduction to line editing ¶

units.text: ⟦0⟧ was created, along with the Unix operating system, by Ken Thompson and Dennis Ritchie. It is the refinement of its more complex, programmable predecessor, ⟦1⟧QED⟦2⟧, to which Thompson and Ritchie had already added pattern matching capabilities (see ⟦3⟧Regular expressions⟦4⟧).
units.sourceHTML: ed was created, along with the Unix operating system, by Ken Thompson and Dennis Ritchie. It is the refinement of its more complex, programmable predecessor, QED, to which Thompson and Ritchie had already added pattern matching capabilities (see Regular expressions).

units.text: For the purposes of this tutorial, a working knowledge of the Unix shell ⟦0⟧ and the Unix file system is recommended, since ⟦1⟧ is designed to interact closely with them. (See the ⟦2⟧bash manual⟦3⟧ for details about bash).
units.sourceHTML: For the purposes of this tutorial, a working knowledge of the Unix shell sh and the Unix file system is recommended, since ed is designed to interact closely with them. (See the bash manual for details about bash).

units.text: The principal difference between line editors and display editors is that display editors provide instant feedback to user commands, whereas line editors require sometimes lengthy input before any effects are seen. The advantage of instant feedback, of course, is that if a mistake is made, it can be corrected immediately, before more damage is done. Editing in ⟦0⟧ requires more strategy and forethought; but if you are up to the task, it can be quite efficient.

Editing in ed requires more strategy and forethought; but if you are up to the task, it can be quite efficient.

units.text: Much of the ⟦0⟧ command syntax is shared with other Unix utilities.
units.sourceHTML: Much of the ed command syntax is shared with other Unix utilities.

units.text: As with the shell, ⟦0⟧RETURN⟦1⟧ (the carriage-return key) enters a line of input. So when we speak of "entering" a command or some text in ⟦2⟧, ⟦3⟧RETURN⟦4⟧ is implied at the end of each line. Prior to typing ⟦5⟧RETURN⟦6⟧, corrections to the line may be made by typing either ⟦7⟧BACKSPACE⟦8⟧ to erase characters backwards, or ⟦9⟧CONTROL⟦10⟧-u (i.e., hold the CONTROL key and type u) to erase the whole line.
units.sourceHTML: As with the shell, RETURN (the carriage-return key) enters a line of input. So when we speak of "entering" a command or some text in ed, RETURN is implied at the end of each line. Prior to typing RETURN, corrections to the line may be made by typing either BACKSPACE to erase characters backwards, or CONTROL-u (i.e., hold the CONTROL key and type u) to erase the whole line.

units.text: So far, this is no different from running commands in the Unix shell. But let’s say we want to edit the output of a command, or save it to a file. First we must capture the command output to a temporary location called a ⟦0⟧buffer⟦1⟧ where ⟦2⟧ can access it. This is done with ⟦3⟧’s ⟦4⟧r⟦5⟧ command (mnemonic: ⟦6⟧read⟦7⟧):

units.text: The sample sessions below illustrate some basic concepts of line editing with ⟦0⟧. We begin by creating a file, ⟦1⟧, with some help from Shakespeare. As with the shell, all input to ⟦2⟧ must be followed by a ⟦3⟧newline⟦4⟧ character. Commands beginning with ‘⟦5⟧’ are taken as comments and ignored. Input mode lines that begin with ‘⟦6⟧’ are just more input.
units.sourceHTML: The sample sessions below illustrate some basic concepts of line editing with ed. We begin by creating a file, sonnet, with some help from Shakespeare. As with the shell, all input to ed must be followed by a newline character. Commands beginning with ‘#’ are taken as comments and ignored. Input mode lines that begin with ‘#’ are just more input.

units.text: Since ⟦0⟧ is line-oriented, we have to tell it which line, or range of lines we want to edit. In the example above, we do this by specifying the line’s number, or sequence in the buffer. Alternatively, we could have specified a unique string in the line, e.g., ‘⟦1⟧’, where the ‘⟦2⟧’s delimit the string in question. Subsequent commands affect only the selected line, a.k.a. the ⟦3⟧current⟦4⟧ line. Portions of that line are then replaced with the substitute command, whose syntax is ‘⟦5⟧’.
units.sourceHTML: Since ed is line-oriented, we have to tell it which line, or range of lines we want to edit. In the example above, we do this by specifying the line’s number, or sequence in the buffer. Alternatively, we could have specified a unique string in the line, e.g., ‘/filvers/’, where the ‘/’s delimit the string in question. Subsequent commands affect only the selected line, a.k.a. the current line. Portions of that line are then replaced with the substitute command, whose syntax is ‘s/old/new/’.

units.text: Although ⟦0⟧ accepts only one command per line, the print command ‘⟦1⟧’ is an exception, and may be appended to the end of most commands.
units.sourceHTML: Although ed accepts only one command per line, the print command ‘p’ is an exception, and may be appended to the end of most commands.

units.text: When ⟦0⟧ opens a file, the current address is initially set to the address of the last line of that file. Similarly, the move command ‘⟦1⟧’ sets the current address to the address of the last line moved.
units.sourceHTML: When ed opens a file, the current address is initially set to the address of the last line of that file. Similarly, the move command ‘m’ sets the current address to the address of the last line moved.
